provisions_triggered.name: Due Process / Law of the Land

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: Before a State may irrevocably sever the parent-child relationship, the Due Process Clause requires the State to prove its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence.
key_cases.relevance: Fixes the federal floor of proof for the Texas termination trial at this node; Texas codified it in Fam. Code § 161.001 and applies it through In re J.F.C. and In re C.H.
key_cases.quote: due process requires that the State support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: A State may not condition an indigent parent's appeal from a termination decree on her ability to pay record-preparation fees.
key_cases.relevance: Guarantees the indigent Texas parent a real appeal from the termination decree; it is the constitutional backstop behind the free record and accelerated appeal in Fam. Code §§ 107.013 and 109.002.
key_cases.quote: Mississippi may not deny M. L. B., because of her poverty, appellate review of the sufficiency of the evidence

key_cases.holding: Legal sufficiency review of a termination finding asks whether a reasonable factfinder could have formed a firm belief or conviction that the ground was proved, viewing the evidence in the light most favorable to the finding.
key_cases.relevance: The governing Texas legal-sufficiency standard for every termination ground and for best interest.
key_cases.quote: look at all the evidence in the light most favorable to the finding to determine whether a reasonable trier of fact could have formed a firm belief

key_cases.holding: Legal and factual sufficiency review of clear-and-convincing findings differ only in how disputed contrary evidence is treated; undisputed contrary evidence can never be disregarded.
key_cases.relevance: The Texas Supreme Court's most recent restatement of the sufficiency standards that control review of a termination decree.
key_cases.quote: In conducting a legal-sufficiency review, the reviewing court cannot ignore undisputed evidence contrary to the finding

key_cases.holding: Because termination of parental rights is of constitutional dimension, involuntary termination statutes are strictly construed in favor of the parent and termination proceedings are strictly scrutinized.
key_cases.relevance: The rule of construction Texas courts apply to every § 161.001 ground: ambiguity in a termination statute is resolved for the parent.
key_cases.quote: termination proceedings should be strictly scrutinized, and involuntary termination statutes are strictly construed in favor of the parent

key_cases.holding: Only one predicate ground under Family Code § 161.001(1), plus a best-interest finding, is needed to support termination; and subsection (Q), which permits termination where a parent will be imprisoned and unable to care for the child for two years, operates prospectively and is constitutional as applied to a parent imprisoned before its effective date.
key_cases.relevance: Fixes the arithmetic of a Texas termination decree: the Department needs one predicate ground plus best interest, so an appellate attack must defeat every ground found. It is also the leading treatment of the (Q) incarceration ground, which nothing else in this brief covers.
key_cases.quote: Only one predicate finding under section 161.001(1) is necessary to support a judgment of termination when there is also a finding that termination is in the child’s best interest.

key_cases.case_name: Texas Department of Human Services v. E.B.
key_cases.holding: In a jury trial to terminate parental rights the controlling question is whether the parent-child relationship should be terminated, and Rule 277 requires that question to be submitted in broad form with the statutory endangerment grounds given as instructions; submitting a single broad-form question covering two independent grounds was not an abuse of discretion.
key_cases.relevance: Sets the shape of the Texas termination jury charge — one broad-form question per child with the § 161.001 grounds as instructions — which is why a Texas verdict rarely reveals which ground the jury relied on.
key_cases.quote: Unless extraordinary circumstances exist, a court must submit such broad-form questions.

key_cases.holding: On legal-sufficiency review of a clear-and-convincing termination finding the court considers all the evidence, not only the evidence favoring the verdict; it disregards contrary evidence a reasonable factfinder could have disbelieved but may not disregard undisputed contrary facts.
key_cases.relevance: Governs the first question on appeal from a termination decree — whether any reasonable factfinder could have formed a firm belief or conviction on the ground found.
key_cases.quote: Therefore, in conducting a legal sufficiency review in a parental termination case, we must consider all of the evidence, not just that which favors the verdict.

key_cases.holding: A parent who opposes a government-initiated termination suit may raise ineffective assistance of counsel on appeal whether counsel was appointed or privately retained; on this record, however, the mother could not show deficient performance under Strickland, so the judgment was affirmed.
key_cases.relevance: Extends the In re M.S. right to effective counsel in a termination to parents who hired their own lawyer — the most common gap in the Texas right-to-counsel scheme, which by its terms only mandates appointment for the indigent.
key_cases.quote: parents may assert a claim for ineffective assistance of counsel, regardless of whether counsel is retained or appointed

key_cases.holding: The statutory right of an indigent parent to appointed counsel under Family Code § 107.013(a)(1) runs through the exhaustion of appeals under § 107.016(2)(B) and therefore includes proceedings in the Supreme Court of Texas, including the petition for review; appointed counsel may satisfy that duty with an Anders-standard petition.
key_cases.relevance: Closes the gap at the end of a termination case: counsel's duty does not stop at the court of appeals, so a parent is not left unrepresented at the only court that can review the intermediate court's decision.
key_cases.quote: we hold that the right to counsel under Section 107.013(a)(1) through the exhaustion of appeals under Section 107.016(2)(B) includes all proceedings in this Court

key_cases.holding: An inmate has no absolute right to appear in person in a civil proceeding; the burden is on the inmate to identify, in the bench-warrant request, the facts showing why his personal appearance is necessary, and a trial court that proceeds without ruling on a request containing no such information does not abuse its discretion.
key_cases.relevance: Governs the incarcerated parent in a Texas termination trial — the single most common reason a respondent parent is physically absent from the hearing that ends his rights.
key_cases.quote: However, an inmate does not have an absolute right to appear in person in every court proceeding.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The State creates a DeShaney 'special relationship' with children when it removes them from their homes and places them under its supervision, assuming a duty of constitutionally adequate care; but that relationship and any liberty interest arising from it lapse when the children are adopted, so the adoptive parents' post-adoption claims for further services failed.
key_cases.relevance: Texas adoption authority: the State's constitutional obligation ends at the adoption decree, which is what makes finalization the true terminus of agency responsibility rather than a continuing guarantee.
key_cases.quote: TDHS created a “special relationship” with the Griffiths’ children when it removed them from their natural homes and placed them under state supervision.

key_cases.case_name: Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians v. Holyfield
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: 'Domicile' under ICWA is a matter of uniform federal law, and twins born off-reservation to parents domiciled on the reservation were themselves domiciled there; the tribal court therefore had exclusive jurisdiction under 25 U.S.C. § 1911(a) and the state adoption decree was vacated.
key_cases.relevance: A Texas termination or adoption decree entered over exclusive tribal jurisdiction is vacatable years later — the strongest collateral-attack risk in any Texas permanency plan involving an Indian child.
key_cases.quote: In enacting the ICWA Congress confirmed that, in child custody proceedings involving Indian children domiciled on the reservation, tribal jurisdiction was exclusive as to the States.

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: ICWA § 1912(f) does not apply where the parent never had custody of the child; § 1912(d)'s active-efforts requirement applies only where terminating the parent's rights would precipitate the breakup of an Indian family; and § 1915(a)'s placement preferences do not bar a non-Indian adoption when no other eligible candidate has sought to adopt.
key_cases.relevance: Determines whether the heightened ICWA burden and active-efforts showing attach at all before a Texas court may terminate and allow an adoption to proceed.
key_cases.quote: Consistent with the statutory text, we hold that §1912(d) applies only in cases where an Indian family’s “breakup” would be precipitated by the termination of the parent’s rights.

search_keywords: Texas Department of Family and Protective Services

state_agency.name: Texas Department of Family and Protective Services

extended_foster_care_age: Up to age 21; to 22 if still completing high school or an equivalency program (voluntary; Tex. Fam. Code § 264.101(a-1)–(a-2))

common_failures: Failure to prove unfitness by clear and convincing evidence
Santosky v. Kramer standard not met

timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Must file TPR or document compelling reason

notice_requirements.timing: Citation on the filing of an original petition shall be issued and served as in other civil cases (Tex. Fam. Code § 102.009(c)); citation by publication, available only for persons entitled to service who cannot be notified by personal service or registered or certified mail and for persons whose names are unknown, must be published not later than the 20th day before the date set for the hearing (Tex. Fam. Code § 102.010(a)-(b))
content_required: Service of citation on the filing of a petition in an original suit is required for each parent as to whom the parent-child relationship has not been terminated or process has not been waived under Chapter 161, an alleged father unless an affidavit of waiver of interest is attached or the petitioner has complied with § 161.002(b)(2), (3), or (4), a man who has filed a notice of intent to claim paternity, a managing or possessory conservator, a person having possession of or access to the child under an order, a guardian of the person or estate of the child, and the Department of Family and Protective Services if the petition requests that it be appointed managing conservator (Tex. Fam. Code § 102.009(a))
Citation may be served on any other person who has or who may assert an interest in the child (Tex. Fam. Code § 102.009(b))

Citation by publication must state that the respondent has been sued, that the respondent may employ an attorney, that a default judgment may be taken unless a written answer is filed with the clerk who issued the citation by 10 a.m. on the Monday next following the expiration of 20 days after service, and the style, number, court, and filing date of the suit (Tex. Fam. Code § 102.010(c))

Immediately after a court renders an order terminating the parent-child relationship in a suit filed by the department, the department must notify each individual identified under § 262.1095 and described by § 102.006(c) that the parent-child relationship has been terminated and that the individual has 90 days after the date the order is rendered to file a suit requesting managing conservatorship (Tex. Fam. Code § 161.2081)
notice_requirements.defective_notice_consequence: Notwithstanding Rule 329, Texas Rules of Civil Procedure, the validity of an order terminating the parental rights of a person who has been personally served, who executed an affidavit of relinquishment or waiver of interest, or whose rights were terminated under § 161.002(b) — and of an order terminating the rights of a person served by citation by publication — is not subject to collateral or direct attack after the sixth month after the date the order was signed (Tex. Fam. Code § 161.211(a)-(b))
